Listen to this article Share A prosecution witness in the N76 billion and $31.5 million fraud trial involving Ahmed Kuru, the former Managing Director, Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON), has told a Lagos court that Kuru approved the appointment of a receiver-manager for Arik Air without obtaining prior approval from the corporation’s board. Bawa Kaltungo, the fourth prosecution witness and acting Zonal Director of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission’s (EFCC) Lagos Zonal Directorate 2, said investigations revealed that the appointment was made before the matter was presented to AMCON’s board for approval. Kaltungo also told the Special Offences Court sitting in Ikeja, Lagos, that the appointments made in connection with the receivership went beyond what the board subsequently approved. The witness gave the testimony on Monday, during cross-examination by Uyi Giwa-Osagie, counsel to Kuru, before Justice Mojisola Dada. Kuru is standing trial alongside Kamilu Alaba Omokide, Roy Ilegbodu, Union Bank of Nigeria Plc and Super Bravo Limited on a six-count charge bordering on alleged conspiracy, stealing and abuse of office. The EFCC accused the defendants of offences connected with the alleged fraudulent transfer of Arik Air’s loans and bank guarantees to AMCON, as well as the alleged conversion of N4.9 billion belonging to the airline for the benefit of NG Eagle Limited. The defendants are being prosecuted over allegations involving N76 billion and $31.5 million. The allegations have yet to be established by the court. Kaltungo, who previously headed the AMCON Desk in Lagos when the investigation commenced, said investigators sought documents establishing that the corporation’s board had approved the appointment of a receiver-manager before the decision was implemented. According to him, the requested documents were not produced during the investigation. He maintained that although AMCON had the authority to appoint a receiver for a company with outstanding debt, the power had to be exercised in accordance with due process. The witness said the investigation sought to establish how AMCON arrived at the decision to appoint a receiver-manager for Arik Air, adding that those responsible for the appointment explained that the airline had an outstanding bad loan. However, he said the EFCC’s investigation found that the claim underlying the receivership arrangement was false. “The evidence gathered by the Commission did not establish that the Nigerian government had paid money to acquire Arik Air or its debt,” Kaltungo told the court. Read also: Court fixes December 2 for judgement in El-Rufai’s N1bn rights suit He explained that the role of a receiver-manager was to take control of a company placed under receivership and protect and preserve its assets. Kaltungo further maintained that the investigation found that AMCON had been misled into taking over what was presented as bad debt, while the commission’s findings indicated that Union Bank of Nigeria Plc had defrauded the corporation in connection with the alleged sale of Arik Air’s loans and bank guarantees. One of the charges against Union Bank alleges that, in 2011, the bank made false statements to AMCON regarding Arik Air Limited’s performing loans, with the intention of inducing the corporation to purchase the airline’s loans and bank guarantees. The charge alleges that the bank subsequently transferred a purported N71 billion figure to AMCON. Another count alleges that Kuru, Omokide, as receiver-manager of Arik Air, and Ilegbodu, as chief executive officer of the airline in receivership, fraudulently converted N4.9 billion belonging to Arik Air to the use of NG Eagle Limited in 2022. Kaltungo told the court that the investigation followed a petition submitted by Femi Falana, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, on behalf of Arik Air’s directors and shareholders. The petition, addressed to the EFCC chairman, was dated April 27, 2023, received by the chairman’s office on May 3, 2023, and forwarded to the commission’s director of operations on May 12, 2023. According to the witness, the EFCC directed the then head of the AMCON Desk to investigate the allegations on May 22, 2023. He said he supervised the investigation alongside other investigators and participated in interviews with individuals considered relevant to the matter. Kaltungo explained that the AMCON Desk was responsible for investigating cases referred to it involving the corporation, although other desks within the commission could also investigate AMCON-related matters. He added that the investigation focused on individuals whose actions were relevant to the allegations rather than solely on the positions they occupied. The witness also identified the investigation report tendered before the court as containing the EFCC’s findings based on the information and evidence available to the commission at the conclusion of its investigation. He said the investigation extended beyond the appointment of the receiver-manager to cover other allegations contained in the petition. The court also heard details about the individuals who served as receiver-managers of Arik Air during the period under investigation. Kaltungo identified Oluseye Opasanya, and Omokide, the second defendant, as the two individuals who had held the position. He told the court that Opasanya ceased to be the receiver-manager in 2019, while Omokide occupied the position when the EFCC conducted its investigation. During cross-examination, Giwa-Osagie presented a document relating to Omokide’s appointment. Kaltungo, however, observed that the copy was incomplete and originated from the Corporate Affairs Commission rather than AMCON. The witness requested the deed of appointment issued by AMCON, which he said had already been submitted to the court as an exhibit. He also told the court that individuals named in the petition worked under the receiver-manager and that responsibility for their actions could arise from the circumstances of the case. Wahab Shittu, counsel to the prosecution, argued that the central issue was whether the board had approved the appointment of the receiver-manager before the decision was implemented. He referred to documents tendered by the defence, including a board resolution dated July 18, 2019, and other documents dated between two and five years after the receivership decision. Shittu argued that although the documents related to the matter, their dates made them too remote to establish that the required approval had been obtained before the appointment. He maintained that the necessary board approval should have been secured before the appointment or within a reasonable period, rather than two to five years after the decision had been taken. In response, Giwa-Osagie argued that the charges against his client related to the appointment of the receiver-manager and maintained that the decisions in question were made by AMCON’s board. He further argued that Kuru was the only board member being prosecuted over the decisions under consideration. Shittu subsequently clarified that the prosecution was not contending that the documents were irrelevant but was challenging their ability to establish prior approval for the decision being investigated. Counsel representing the second, third, fourth and fifth defendants informed the court that they had no objections to the seven documents tendered by counsel to the first defendant. After hearing arguments from the prosecution and defence, Dada admitted the documents containing AMCON board resolutions in evidence.
